claims.text: The modified Cantor alloy coating has a dual-phase microstructure containing both FCC and HCP phases.
Tailoring composition and processing can precisely control the proportions of metastable phases in the multilayer coating.
Controlled metastable phase proportions produce robust FCC/HCP phase boundaries.
Controlled metastable phase proportions promote the development of stacking-fault networks.
FCC/HCP phase boundaries and associated stacking-fault networks act as effective barriers to dislocations.
Dislocation barriers created by the dual-phase architecture reduce time-dependent plastic deformation relative to single-phase coatings.
Interfaces in the dual-phase structure serve as strong dislocation-pinning sites.
Dynamic transformation-induced plasticity enhances strain hardening in the dual-phase coating.
The combination of interface pinning and transformation-induced plasticity hinders dislocation motion.
The combination of interface pinning and transformation-induced plasticity delays strain localization during creep.
Engineered dual-phase multilayers will have lower creep rates than monolithic or single-phase coatings.
Engineered dual-phase multilayers will exhibit greater strain hardening than monolithic or single-phase coatings.
The proposed resistance mechanism is anticipated to operate from 298 to 573 K.
The proposed effect applies only where a controlled metastable FCC+HCP structure is achievable.
Processing-induced shifts away from the targeted metastable phase balance may alter the creep response.
The hypothesis can be tested by comparing dual-phase multilayers with monolithic single-phase HEA coatings using creep tests and in-situ microscopy or diffraction.
A lack of statistically significant creep-rate reduction or strain-hardening enhancement relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe effective dislocation pinning at phase boundaries would falsify the proposed mechanism.
